title: Access Token Manipulation: Parent PID Spoofing
shortTitle: Access Token Manipulation: Parent PID Spoofing
summary: Parent process identifier spoofing abuses the fact that the recorded parent of a Windows process is a value the creating code can choose rather than a fact Windows always derives. The process creation interface accepts a parameter that names the process to record as the parent, and specialised helper utilities exist that do the same from a command line. Because the parent identifier is a number that gets reused after processes exit, the chosen value can point at any live process, so a malicious child appears in logs and in process monitor trees as the descendant of a trusted binary while the real creator never appears. Windows itself relies on this mechanism when User Account Control has SYSTEM spawn an elevated process, which is why the behaviour cannot be judged on the mismatch alone. The strongest artefacts are logical contradictions rather than the interface: a child whose creation timestamp precedes the recorded parent, a parent-child pair whose identifier belongs to a process on another session, process trees in endpoint telemetry with a missing link, and children that claim an office or explorer parent but carry a command line no document viewer would produce.

beginner.definition: Every program on Windows records which program started it, and that record is called the parent. An attacker can set that value to a program of their choice, so a harmful program looks like it was started by a trusted one. The real creator stays hidden from tools that trust the record.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many defences block or flag programs that are started by office documents or email clients. If the record says the parent was a normal desktop program, those rules do not fire. Investigators reading logs then draw the wrong conclusion about how an infection happened. The program itself can also inherit power from a parent that runs as the SYSTEM account.
howItWorks: Windows normally records the program that called for a new process as its parent.
The Windows process creation function also accepts a chosen parent value instead.
Attacker code calls that function directly and supplies a trusted program as the parent.
Security tools and logs then show the harmful program as a child of the trusted one.
The attacker may also point the parent at a powerful process such as lsass, which holds login data.
If the parent runs as SYSTEM, the child can receive stronger rights when it starts.
beginner.example: Think of an airport queue where each passenger must say who invited them. A traveller writes the name of a trusted airline employee on the form. The queue officer checks the name against a staff list, finds it valid, and waves the traveller through. Nobody calls the employee to confirm. The traveller entered the country on someone else good name.
takeaways: The parent recorded for a process is an input, so it can be deliberately wrong.
Check timing and session details, because a real parent must exist before its child starts.
Spoofing lineage also lets a child inherit power from a parent running as SYSTEM.

objectives: Explain what a parent process identifier is and why the value can be chosen by the creating code.
Describe how spoofing a parent evades defences that inspect process relationships.
Explain how a spoofed parent can lead to stronger privileges through an inherited token.
Identify the contradictions in process telemetry that expose a false parent.
Explain why Windows itself legitimately assigns parents to elevated processes.
